title: Sublimation, crossing parity, and the full phase criterion
html:
Remark. Sublimation, crossing parity, and the full phase criterion

The single Hecke algebra H_n(q) of prop:composite-crossing-parity governs the phase behaviour through the following criteria.

Sublimation criterion. There is no split/non-split dichotomy to state this criterion in. At a substrate parameter that is not a root of unity H_n(q) is semisimple, so every short exact sequence of H_n(q)-modules splits and \mathrm{Ext}^1_{H_n(q)} vanishes on every pair of modules (prop:phase-transition-boundary); the S_\lambda are irreducible summands of V^{\otimes n} (prop:knot-eigenbasis-complete(1)), and an irreducible module is not an extension of anything by anything.

What is left is a correlation with the Young diagram of the valence shell, stated without a mechanism. The liquid phase is stable when the outermost electron shell is closed or nearly closed — in terms of partitions, when the diagram \lambda_{\mathrm{outer}} labelling the valence electrons satisfies \lambda_1 - \lambda_2 \leq 1, so that the valence shell inhabits the symmetric or near-symmetric sector of the Schur--Weyl decomposition. Sublimation is instead associated with a half-filled valence shell (\lambda_1 \approx \lambda_2 + n/2), where the mixed Hecke channel achieves maximal dimension. That dimension statement is a fact about S_\lambda; the step from it to a thermodynamic instability is not supplied here.

Crossing parity. To estimate sublimation behavior, we examine the composite crossing parity. The composite crossing number identically satisfies n_K(\mathcal{A}) \equiv Z \pmod{2}, stemming from the crossing budget A^2 + 7A + 5Z and the invariant parity A(A+1) \equiv 0 \pmod{2}. This parity detects the mod-2 shadow of the Young diagram structure. It acts as a necessary but not sufficient condition for sublimation, as it fails to distinguish closed shells from half-filled ones.

Full criterion. Let \ell_v denote the number of valence electrons beyond the last closed shell. Let \ell_{\max} dictate the capacity of the valence shell (\ell_{\max} = 2n^2 for principal quantum number n). We systematically classify the macroscopic phase:

  1. Closed shell (\ell_v = 0 or \ell_v = \ell_{\max}): The liquid phase is stable.
  2. Near-closed shell (\ell_v = 1 or \ell_v = \ell_{\max} - 1): The liquid phase is stable.
  3. Half-filled shell (\ell_v \approx \ell_{\max}/2) with odd Z: The atom is structurally prone to sublimation.
  4. Metallic band (delocalized electrons): The single-atom Hecke module S_\lambda expands to the band-structure module \bigoplus_k S_{\lambda(k)} over crystal momenta k, and the liquid phase is stable.

The classification is empirical: nothing above derives it from the Hecke representation theory.
